verses.context: God's first recorded word to Abram. After the scattering at Babel and the family's halt in Haran (11:31), the LORD speaks, and the story narrows from all nations to one man. The command asks Abram to give up three circles of belonging and names no destination.
verses.grammar: Lekh lekha, “Leave”, is an imperative of halakh (‘go’) followed by lekha, ‘for yourself’ or ‘by yourself’. Grammarians call this kind of added pronoun an ethical or reflexive dative; it focuses the action on the one addressed, and interpreters have heard in it either ‘go for your own good’ or ‘go, you yourself, alone’. The three things to leave narrow as they go: land, kindred (moledet), and father's household. Arekka, “I will show you”, is a Hiphil imperfect of raah, ‘cause to see’: the land will be shown, not described in advance. Some older translations, such as the King James Version, render the opening ‘had said’, placing this call back in Ur in line with 15:7 and Acts 7:2; most modern versions keep the simple sequence.

theology.note: The command comes before any explanation of where or why. Abram is asked to act on God's word alone, which is why Hebrews 11:8 makes his departure a model of faith: he went out not knowing where he was going.

verses.context: The first half of the promise. God pledges to make Abram a great nation, to bless him, and to make his name great. The builders of Babel tried to make a name for themselves (11:4); here God gives a great name to a man who has not asked for one.
verses.grammar: The first three verbs are first person forms with the conjunction, expressing God's resolve: ‘I will make you... I will bless you... I will make great your name’. Then comes a surprise: veheyeh berakhah is an imperative, literally ‘and be a blessing’. After a string of first person promises, a following imperative often expresses the intended result, which is why the BSB renders it “so that you will be a blessing”. The blessing of Abram is not an end in itself; its purpose is that he become a channel of blessing.

theology.note: The promises of nationhood, blessing, and a great name are given before Abram has done anything. They become the substance of the covenant ratified in chapter 15, and the promise of a great name returns in God's covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:9).

verses.context: The second half of the promise turns outward. God will bless those who bless Abram and curse whoever treats him with contempt, and through him all the families of the earth will be blessed. The verse answers the list of families in chapter 10 and the scattering of chapter 11.
verses.grammar: The final clause, venivrekhu vekha, uses the Niphal of barakh, which is normally passive: ‘they will be blessed through you’. When the promise is repeated to Abraham after the binding of Isaac (22:18) and to Isaac (26:4), the verb is a Hithpael, a form that more naturally means ‘bless themselves’, that is, use Abraham's name when invoking blessing. The Niphal returns in 18:18 and 28:14. The Greek translation and the New Testament (Galatians 3:8; Acts 3:25) read the passive sense. The phrase for the earth is haadamah, the ‘ground’ that was cursed in 3:17: the families of the cursed ground are to be blessed.

theology.note: The goal of Abram's calling is universal. The chosen family exists for the sake of the families of the whole earth, and Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8).

verses.context: Abram goes. The narrator reports no reply, no question, and no hesitation, only obedience that matches the command. Lot goes with him, though the call did not name him, and the age of seventy-five marks the moment.
verses.grammar: Vayyelekh, “departed”, repeats the verb of the command (lekh, ‘go’), so the obedience answers the command word for word. The clause ‘as the LORD had directed him’ (kaasher dibber) is the formula Genesis used for Noah's obedience (6:22; 7:9). The age is given with the phrase ben ... shanah, literally ‘a son of seventy-five years’, the usual Hebrew idiom for age.

theology.note: Faith here is simply walking where God has spoken. The man who has no child and no land sets out at seventy-five on the strength of a promise of both.

verses.context: Abram takes his household and property and this time reaches the goal. Terah's party set out for Canaan and stopped at Haran (11:31); Abram's party sets out for Canaan and arrives. The repetition of ‘the land of Canaan’ at the end of the verse marks the difference.
verses.grammar: “Possessions” translates rekhush, movable property, especially livestock, and the verb rakhashu (‘they had acquired’) is from the same root, a sound pattern that stresses their wealth. The “people” are literally hannefesh asher asu, ‘the persons they had made’. The verb asah (‘make’) is used here in the sense of acquiring, as in 31:1, and the persons are the household's servants and dependents. Rabbinic interpreters, followed by Rashi, read the phrase as the people Abram and Sarai had brought to faith in God.

verses.context: Abram passes through the land to Shechem, in its central hills. The narrator notes that the Canaanites were then in the land: the promised land is occupied, and Abram enters it as a stranger.
verses.grammar: “Traveled through” is vayyaavor, from avar, ‘to pass through’, the verb later used for Israel crossing the Jordan into the same land (Joshua 3:14-17). The tree is elon moreh, probably a large oak or terebinth. Moreh is a participle-like form of yarah, ‘to teach’ or ‘to direct’, so the name may mean ‘the teacher's tree’ or ‘the oracle tree’. The adverb az (“at that time”) can also mean ‘already’: even then, the Canaanites were there.
verses.history: Shechem is identified with Tell Balata, beside modern Nablus, in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. It was a major walled city in the Middle Bronze Age, is mentioned in Egyptian texts of the second millennium BC, and became the place of Joshua's covenant renewal (Joshua 24:1, 25-26), where a great tree by the sanctuary is again named.

verses.context: In the middle of a land held by others, the LORD appears and promises it to Abram's offspring. Abram answers with an altar. The promise of the land, only implied in verse 1, is now stated.
verses.grammar: Vayyera, “appeared”, is a Niphal of raah, ‘to be seen’. This is the first time Scripture says the LORD appeared to someone, and the altar is dedicated to ‘the LORD who had appeared to him’, using the same verb as a participle (hannireh). In the promise the Hebrew puts lezarakha, “to your offspring”, first for emphasis. Zera (‘seed’) is a collective singular, meaning descendants; Paul builds an argument on its singular form in Galatians 3:16, reading it in light of Christ.

theology.note: The land promise is given to Abram's descendants, not to Abram. Stephen notes that God gave Abraham no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground, yet promised it to him and his offspring (Acts 7:5). The promise looks beyond the one who first receives it.

verses.context: Abram moves south into the hills between Bethel and Ai, pitches his tent, builds a second altar, and calls on the LORD's name. Tent and altar together describe his life in the land: temporary shelter for himself, a place of worship for God.
verses.grammar: Vayyatteq, “moved on”, is a Hiphil of ataq, ‘to shift’ or ‘to move along’. The directions are given as an Israelite would give them: miyyam, ‘from the sea’, for west, and miqqedem for east. “Called on the name of the LORD” (vayyiqra beshem YHWH) repeats the phrase first used in 4:26 for the beginning of public worship. It means to worship and pray to God by his name, not merely to mention it.
verses.history: Bethel is usually located at Beitin, about 19 kilometers (12 miles) north of Jerusalem; Ai, whose name means ‘the ruin’ and always has the article in Hebrew, is traditionally placed at et-Tell nearby, though that identification is debated because of the site's occupation history. The narrator uses the name Bethel, which Jacob will give the place later (28:19); before that it was called Luz.

theology.note: Abram's life in the land is marked by public worship. Calling on the LORD's name at an altar, where others could see it, declares whose land this is and whose protection he trusts.

verses.context: Abram keeps moving south toward the Negev. The verse closes the first half of the chapter with a man who has not settled anywhere: he lives in the land of promise by moving through it.
verses.grammar: Halokh venasoa pairs two infinitive absolutes after the main verb, ‘going and setting out’, the construction used for continuing action (compare 8:3). Nasa literally means to pull up tent pegs, so it describes travel by stages, from camp to camp. Hannegbah, ‘toward the Negev’, has the directional ending -ah. Negev comes from a root meaning dry, and because the Negev lay south of Israel's heartland the word also became the ordinary Hebrew for ‘south’.
verses.history: The Negev is the semi-arid region of southern Israel around Beersheba, fit for grazing flocks in the rainy season but hard to farm. It will become a home base for Abraham and Isaac (20:1; 24:62) and is the first region to feel a failure of the winter rains.

verses.context: A famine strikes the land God has just promised. Abram goes down to Egypt to live there for a time. The text records no word from God and no altar here; the decision is Abram's.
verses.grammar: Vayyered, “went down”, is the usual way of speaking about travel from the hill country of Canaan to Egypt, and it is the same verb the story of Joseph and Jacob will use (42:3; 46:3-4). Lagur, ‘to sojourn’, means to live as a resident foreigner, not to settle permanently. The famine was kaved, literally ‘heavy’, the same word used later for Pharaoh's heavy or hardened heart (Exodus 7:14).
verses.history: Egypt did not depend on rain, because the Nile's yearly flood watered its fields. An Egyptian administrative letter of the late thirteenth century BC (Papyrus Anastasi VI) records a frontier official allowing pastoral tribes from Edom to pass a border fortress into the eastern delta to keep themselves and their herds alive, the same kind of movement this verse describes.

verses.context: At the border Abram lays out his plan. He expects the Egyptians to kill him to take Sarai, and he asks her to say she is his sister so that he will be well treated and his life spared. His concern is for himself; he does not ask what will happen to her.
verses.grammar: Abram's speech is polite and urgent: hinneh na, “Look”, and imri na, ‘say, please’, both carry the particle na, which softens a request. Verse 12 lays out his expected future in a chain of consecutive perfects: they will see, they will say, they will kill. The purpose clause in verse 13, lemaan yitav li, ‘so that it may go well for me’, and the closing vechayetah nafshi biglalekh, ‘and my life will live because of you’, put his own safety at the center twice.

theology.note: The same man who left everything at God's word now plans for survival as though God had promised nothing. Genesis records the lapse without softening it, and the pattern returns in 20:2 and with Isaac in 26:7. Faith in Scripture grows through failures like this one.

verses.context: Everything happens as Abram predicted, except the killing. The Egyptians notice Sarai, the officials praise her to Pharaoh, and she is taken into his household. Abram is treated well for her sake and grows rich.
verses.grammar: Vayhallelu, “commended”, is the Piel of halal, the verb that elsewhere means ‘praise’ (as in hallelujah); the officials praise Sarai as a prize. Vattuqqach, “was taken”, is a Hophal, a passive form: Sarai is acted on and never speaks in the whole episode. Heitiv, ‘he did good’, in verse 16 echoes Abram's own words in verse 13, yitav li, ‘that it may go well for me’. His plan works exactly as he hoped, and the text lets the reader feel what it has cost.
verses.history: The gifts listed are those of a wealthy herding household, and the menservants and maidservants may include Hagar, the Egyptian servant who appears in 16:1. On the camels, see the chapter note: whether they belong to Abram's time or reflect the narrator's day is debated.

verses.context: The LORD intervenes. Pharaoh and his household are struck with great plagues because of Sarai, whom the narrator names pointedly as Abram's wife. The promise that depends on her is protected by God, not by Abram.
verses.grammar: Vaynagga ... negaim, ‘he plagued with plagues’, pairs a Piel of naga (‘to strike’, ‘to touch’) with its own noun. Nega is the word used in Exodus 11:1 for the last plague on Egypt, so the story previews the exodus. The phrase al devar sarai, ‘on account of the matter of Sarai’, keeps the focus on her, and the title ‘the wife of Abram’ states the fact Abram had hidden.

theology.note: God guards the promise even when its bearer endangers it. Psalm 105:14-15 looks back on the patriarchs' travels and says God rebuked kings for their sake, telling them not to touch his anointed ones.

verses.context: Pharaoh summons Abram and questions him three times. The pagan king speaks with moral clarity; the man of promise says nothing. Pharaoh returns Sarai and orders Abram to go.
verses.grammar: Mah zot asita li, “What have you done to me?”, is the same kind of question God asked in 3:13, and it returns on other lips in 20:9, 26:10, and 29:25. The two ‘why’ questions (lamah) that follow expose the half-truth. “So that I took her as my wife” is a wayyiqtol, vaeqqach, which reports the taking as an event that followed from Abram's words. The text does not say whether the marriage was consummated, while in the parallel story of 20:4-6 it says plainly that Abimelech had not touched her. Pharaoh's closing commands, kach valekh, ‘take and go’, are blunt.

theology.note: Abram was called to be a blessing to the nations, and his first encounter with a foreign nation brings it plagues instead. The episode shows how the bearers of God's promise can obscure it, and how the outsider can be the one who speaks the truth.

verses.context: Pharaoh gives orders, and his men escort Abram out of Egypt with Sarai and everything he owns. The chapter that began with God sending Abram ends with Pharaoh sending him away.
verses.grammar: Vayshallechu, “sent him away”, is the Piel of shalach, ‘to send off’ or ‘to let go’. It is the verb of the exodus demand, ‘Let My people go’ (Exodus 5:1, shallach), and of Pharaoh's final release of Israel (Exodus 12:33). Vaytsav (‘gave orders’) is the Piel of tsavah, used here of a royal command and escort.

theology.note: The pattern of Israel's future is sketched in Abram's life: famine, descent to Egypt, danger, plagues, and departure with wealth. The God who brings Abram out of Egypt will bring his descendants out in the same way (Exodus 12:35-36).
